title: Elizabeth of Portugal (4 July)
hookLine: a queen who rode between armies to make peace

lines: A QUEEN RIDES INTO THE MIDDLE.
cards: Two armies face each other across a field. On one side, a king. On the other, his own son, who has risen against him.
Banners, horses, men waiting for the signal. And then, tradition says, a woman on a mule rides out alone into the open ground between them. She is the king's wife and the rebel's mother.
She stops there and won't move until they talk. Today, the queen in the middle. Elizabeth of Portugal.

teach.h: A QUEEN IN A HARD MARRIAGE.
teach.b: Elizabeth was a princess of Aragon, in Spain, married young to King Denis of Portugal. The marriage wasn't easy. Denis was a capable king, and an unfaithful husband.

Elizabeth's lives tell of her raising his children by other women alongside her own, and of a quiet, stubborn life of prayer and care for the poor in the middle of a royal court. In public, her work was peace.
When her son Afonso rose against his father, the kingdom came close to war between them.

Elizabeth went back and forth, pleading with each, and at least once, tradition says, she rode between the two armies to stop the battle before it began. She also helped settle quarrels between Portugal and its neighbors.
Jesus says it in the Sermon on the Mount. In the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Notice what a peacemaker in this story actually does.
Not a speech from a safe distance.

teach.h: HER OWN BODY IN THE GAP.
teach.b: She puts her own body in the gap, loving both sides too much to let either win by killing the other. There's a gentler legend too.

teach.h: BREAD IN THE CLOAK, THEN ROSES.
teach.b: Tradition says she was carrying bread to the poor in her cloak when the king stopped her and asked what she had.

She opened the cloak, and it was full of roses. The same story is told of another royal Elizabeth, her great-aunt in Hungary, and many readers take it as a picture: charity hidden, and turned to beauty when questioned.
After Denis died, Elizabeth gave herself to prayer and service beside the Poor Clares, and tradition says she died while traveling to make peace yet again.

how: The Church keeps an optional memorial of Saint Elizabeth of Portugal on 4 July; in Portugal, above all in Coimbra where she is buried, she is honored as the Holy Queen, and Catholics ask her prayers for peace in families and between nations.

o: a queen of Hungary who founded the Poor Clares
a queen of Portugal who made peace in her own family
a Spanish abbess who wrote the first rule for nuns

games.q: you're the queen. your husband and your son have armies facing each other across a field. what do you do?
o: stay in the palace and wait for news.
ride out into the space between the armies.
back the side most likely to win.
games.why: tradition says Elizabeth rode out between the two armies, and the battle was stopped before it began.

practice: Bring to mind two people who aren't speaking, or keep clashing; maybe you're one of them.
Without taking a side, hold each with the same care, as Elizabeth held a husband and a son, and wonder what one honest step toward the middle might look like.
If you pray, hold them both before God; if you don't, keep them both in mind without choosing.

carryVoice: Your line: the peacemaker queen. Sometimes peace needs someone standing right in the middle. I'll be here tomorrow.
